Quantum mechanics

 Home Physics Branches of physics
OurBigBook.com Words: 77k Articles: 1k
Quantum mechanics describes a quantum system using a quantum state, with observables represented by self-adjoint operators. For a single particle in one dimension, a pure state can be described by a wavefunction ψ(x,t): its squared modulus gives the probability density for position. The Schrödinger equation predicts how this probability amplitude evolves between interventions; measurement in quantum mechanics connects it to experimental outcomes through the Born rule. A wavefunction therefore predicts a distribution of possible positions rather than a single trajectory as in classical mechanics.
The infinite square well makes three central ideas visible with elementary sine functions. Confinement selects discrete energy eigenvalues; wavefunction normalization converts a shape into quantitative probabilities; and a quantum superposition can have a changing probability density even when each constituent energy eigenstate has a stationary one. This combination explains why quantum mechanics uses both linear algebra and differential equations: eigenfunctions describe the building blocks, while quantum phases determine how they interfere. The same tools help explain the discrete energies of chemical atoms and molecules, although their Quantum Hamiltonians require different potentials and often many particles.
In his first 1926 paper, Erwin Schrödinger formulated quantization as an eigenvalue problem for a hydrogen atom in nonrelativistic quantum mechanics. On its opening page he compared the emergence of integers with the number of nodes of a standing wave on a vibrating string. The infinite square well below realizes that appealing idea especially transparently: the allowed integers follow from the boundary conditions. This historical analogy concerns the origin of discrete energies; the Born rule supplies the statistical interpretation of the modern wavefunction. [ref].

Energy-level degeneracy (g)

Words: 24
Quantum mechanics OurBigBook.com
The number of independent quantum states sharing one energy eigenvalue. A level of angular momentum J has 2J+1 magnetic substates when no interaction splits them.

Magnetic-gradient quartic confinement (Vk​(x)=[ℏk−qαx2/2]2/(2m))

Words: 243 Articles: 3
Quantum mechanics OurBigBook.com
A spinless charged particle in Bz​=αx admits vector potential Ay​=αx2/2. Separating a plane wave along y produces a one-dimensional quartic potential energy. For nonzero qα, k/(qα)>0 gives two minima at ±2ℏk/(qα)​; the opposite sign gives one minimum at zero. The field gradient creates confinement even though there is no scalar potential. The quartic potential is even, so its nondegenerate eigenstates have definite spatial parity.

Double-well oscillator scale in a linear magnetic field (ωd​=2ℏqαk​/m)

Words: 118 Articles: 1
Magnetic-gradient quartic confinement OurBigBook.com
For qαk>0, let x0​=2ℏk/(qα)​. Expansion of the magnetic-gradient quartic confinement at either minimum gives V(x0​+δx)=(qα)2x02​(δx)2/(2m)+⋯. The local oscillator frequency is therefore ∣qα∣x0​/m. Both lowest parity states have leading energy ℏωd​/2 if x0​ greatly exceeds the oscillator width. Local anharmonicity changes their common energy, while quantum tunnelling gives their much smaller splitting.

Signed group velocity of a magnetic-gradient doublet (vy​=ℏqα/[2m2ℏqαk​])

Words: 64
Double-well oscillator scale in a linear magnetic field OurBigBook.com
Differentiating Ek​≃ℏ3qαk/2​/m gives the displayed group velocity when qαk>0. Its sign is the sign of qα, equivalently of k on that branch. Writing only a positive square root of qα/k would lose this sign. Exactly, the Hellmann–Feynman theorem gives vy​=⟨ℏk−qαx2/2⟩/m. Evaluating this small drift from a localized wavefunction requires enough anharmonic accuracy: a leading centred Gaussian alone need not reproduce it.

Translation separation in a magnetic field gradient

Words: 58
Magnetic-gradient quartic confinement OurBigBook.com
In a gauge with potentials independent of y, the canonical momentum py​ commutes with the Hamiltonian. A simultaneous eigenbasis can be chosen as eikyΦk​(x), with py​=ℏk. Periodic length Ly​ gives k=2πn/Ly​. The kinetic y-momentum is instead ℏk−qAy​(x) and is not spatially constant. Confusing these two momenta loses the magnetic contribution to the velocity.

Relativistic quantum mechanics

Words: 25
Quantum mechanics OurBigBook.com
A description of quantum states and dynamics compatible with special relativity. Relativistic one-particle equations have a useful domain, while interactions that create or destroy particles generally require quantum field theory.

Bipartite quantum system (HAB​=HA​⊗HB​)

Words: 34
Quantum mechanics OurBigBook.com
A quantum system with two specified subsystems has a tensor product Hilbert space. A joint density operator determines subsystem A's measurement statistics through its partial trace ρA​=TrB​ρAB​. A joint pure state need not give a pure reduced state: the Bell state (∣00⟩+∣11⟩)/2​ gives ρA​=I/2.

Quantum virial theorem

Words: 25
Quantum mechanics OurBigBook.com
For a stationary bound state with suitable operator domains, 2⟨K⟩=⟨x⋅∇V⟩. In a quadratic harmonic potential this gives ⟨K⟩=⟨V⟩=E/2.

Quantum transport

Words: 571 Articles: 14
Quantum mechanics OurBigBook.com
Transport of particles or charge when quantum mode structure, transmission and occupation of reservoir states determine the measured current.

Universal conductance fluctuations (δG∼e2/h)

Words: 49
Quantum transport OurBigBook.com
A coherent disordered mesoscopic conductor has reproducible, sample-dependent conductance variations when magnetic field, carrier energy or disorder configuration changes. Their typical scale is of order e2/h in a fully coherent diffusive sample, with numerical factors determined by symmetry, dimensionality and geometry. Thermal averaging and finite phase coherence length reduce the measured amplitude.

Phase coherence length (Lϕ​)

Words: 38
Quantum transport OurBigBook.com
The characteristic distance over which phase-breaking processes suppress electron-path interference. For diffusion, Lϕ​∼Dτϕ​​; ballistic phase propagation instead gives a scale vτϕ​. This differs from the elastic mean free path, since elastic scattering can change momentum while retaining coherence.

Quasi-one-dimensional quantum transport

Words: 97 Articles: 1
Quantum transport OurBigBook.com
A narrow conductor has discrete transverse modes and nearly continuous longitudinal motion. Its conductance depends on the transmissions of occupied quantum wire subbands, spin counting and contacts. The Landauer formula connects these transmissions to two-terminal conductance. Disorder, interference, dephasing and interactions distinguish ballistic, diffusive, localized and interacting regimes.

Transverse electronic mode

Words: 53
Quasi-one-dimensional quantum transport OurBigBook.com
A transverse confinement eigenstate that defines a threshold for propagation along a narrow conductor. Above that threshold, its longitudinal dispersion supplies an incident channel from each reservoir. spin can label separate channels; an unresolved spin-degenerate mode contributes twice the single-spin spin-resolved conductance quantum. This physical use of mode is unrelated to the most probable value of a probability distribution.

Landauer formula

Words: 368 Articles: 9
Quantum transport OurBigBook.com
A transport expression relating current to occupied incident modes and their transmission probabilities. For spin-degenerate independent electrons, I=(2e/h)∑i​∫Ti​(E)[fL​(E)−fR​(E)]dE, with the direction convention chosen consistently. In linear response a perfectly transmitted mode contributes 2e2/h.

Flux-normalized transmission matrix

Words: 38 Articles: 1
Landauer formula OurBigBook.com
An element tnm​ is the amplitude for an incident unit-flux channel m to emerge in outgoing unit-flux channel n. Then ∣tnm​∣2 is a transmission probability and tr(t†t) sums transmitted channels. Unnormalized wave amplitudes require velocity ratios.
Spin channel counting in a transmission trace
Flux-normalized transmission matrix OurBigBook.com

Spin-resolved conductance quantum

Words: 55 Articles: 1
Landauer formula OurBigBook.com
A perfectly transmitted spin-resolved channel contributes e2/h to two-terminal linear conductance. Two degenerate spin channels give 2e2/h. Flux normalization cancels group velocity against the longitudinal state density.
Thermally rounded channel threshold
Words: 27
Spin-resolved conductance quantum OurBigBook.com
For perfect transmission above threshold En​, integrating −df/dE gives Gn​=(e2/h)f(En​). Thermal occupation rounds a zero-temperature conductance step over an energy range of order kB​T.

Flux carried by a directed electronic mode (dN˙=dE/h)

Words: 58
Landauer formula OurBigBook.com
For one directed spin-resolved channel, the density of longitudinal states per unit length and wave number is 1/(2π). Since v=ℏ−1dE/dk, velocity times density per energy is 1/h. A reservoir occupation imbalance therefore contributes particle flux ∫δf(E)dE/h; in zero-temperature linear response it is δμ/h. Multiplying by charge and transmission gives the Landauer current per mode.

Landauer-Büttiker formula (Ii​=(e2/h)[Ni​Vi​−∑j​Tij​Vj​])

Words: 154 Articles: 2
Landauer formula OurBigBook.com
A multi-reservoir quantum transport relation. Here Ii​ is conventional current injected from reservoir i, Ni​ counts outgoing spin-resolved modes and Tij​ counts transmission from reservoir j into i. Postulates of quantum mechanics

Words: 113
Quantum mechanics OurBigBook.com
For an isolated quantum system, pure states are normalized rays in a complex Hilbert space, observables are self-adjoint operators, and their probabilities obey the Born rule. A spectral projector Pa​ has outcome probability ⟨ψ∣Pa​∣ψ⟩; an ideal repeatable projective measurement has conditional state Pa​ψ/⟨ψ∣Pa​∣ψ⟩​. The Schrödinger equation specifies continuous unitary evolution between such ideal measurements, given a Hamiltonian operator. General measurements need not have the projective state-update rule.
Composite systems use the tensor product of their state spaces. Identical particles additionally obey the bosonic or fermionic exchange symmetry appropriate to their species. The photoelectric effect, Davisson–Germer experiment and double-slit experiment motivate energy quanta, matter-wave phases and probability interference, respectively; these experiments constrain the framework but do not separately prove every abstract postulate or specify every system's Hamiltonian.

Operator formalism

The operator formalism describes a quantum system using states in a Hilbert space and observables represented by self-adjoint operators with suitable domains on that Hilbert space. The operator-path-integral equivalence relates these matrix elements to integrals over field histories.

Matrix mechanics

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Operator formalism OurBigBook.com
Matrix mechanics represents an observable by an array of matrix elements between chosen quantum states. In an orthonormal basis of energy eigenstates, each a stationary state, the diagonal entries of the Hamiltonian operator are the energy levels; off-diagonal entries of other observables describe couplings between those states. The same array can therefore answer two different questions: which values can a measurement return, and which pairs of energy eigenstates can a specified interaction connect? The eigenvalues answer the first question; the relevant matrix elements, together with the energy differences, answer the second.
This makes linear algebra a practical language for atomic physics. One can calculate energy levels, electric-dipole selection rules and probability amplitudes for transitions without assigning an electron an unobserved classical orbit. The three-state example below separates a missing optical coupling from a missing energy level; the finite oscillator commutator boundary defect explains why a finite array requires care when approximating a quantum harmonic oscillator.

A matrix element can be negative or complex; by itself it is not generally a probability. The Born rule assigns measurement probabilities using the eigenstates of A, which need not be energy eigenstates. For an unbounded observable, these expressions require a suitable operator domain; a system with continuous spectrum also needs the corresponding spectral integrals.

From Heisenberg arrays to Born-Jordan commutation

Words: 227
Matrix mechanics OurBigBook.com
In 1925, Werner Heisenberg proposed replacing classical orbital quantities with arrays of transition amplitudes and frequencies. His paper's opening demanded relations between quantities observable in principle; section 1 built products by summing over an intermediate state and noted their dependence on order. The formulas above express that construction in modern linear operator notation.[ref]
Pumping and a heated bath prepared Mercury vapor around a hot platinum wire, mesh and collector in the original Franck-Hertz experiment. A galvanometer read collector electric current while accelerating voltage varied at fixed retarding voltage. Retarding scans distinguished outgoing electron energies.[ref] The losses constrain excitation of chemical atoms; they do not determine every optical coupling. The Franck-Hertz experiment explains the original mistaken ionization interpretation.
Such excitation and spectral line evidence motivated a mechanics of discrete energy levels and transitions. Replacing one representation by another was a theoretical construction; the Franck-Hertz experiment does not measure a matrix product or establish a unique representation of an observable.
Later in 1925, Max Born and Pascual Jordan developed the array calculus systematically. Their section 3 states pq−qp=hI/(2πi), equivalently the modern canonical commutation relation
[X,P]=iℏI.
(11)
This relates position and momentum through an intrinsically noncommuting product.[ref]
For the quantum harmonic oscillator, the canonical commutation relation and creation and annihilation operators give H=ℏω(a†a+I/2), recovering both the spacing and zero-point energy algebraically. One must retain infinitely many number states for the exact relation: the finite cutoff below reveals the obstruction explicitly.

His paper connected wave mechanics with matrix mechanics; the translation's sections 2–3 develop the product and commutation rules.[ref]
The modern proof is a change of orthonormal basis. If ϕn​(x) form a complete orthonormal basis of the physical Hilbert space, map a wavefunction to its coefficients:
cn​=∫ϕn​(x)∗ψ(x)dx,Amn​=∫ϕm​(x)∗(Aϕn​)(x)dx.
(12)
Completeness makes this map unitary: it preserves the inner product and reconstructs ψ from its coefficients. Inserting the complete orthonormal basis proves the matrix multiplication rule. The Schrödinger equation becomes
iℏc˙m​=∑n​Hmn​cn​.
(13)
For a time-independent Hamiltonian operator, the Heisenberg picture transfers the same evolution to the observables, preserving measurement predictions. Unitary equivalence requires matching operator domains as well as formal entries. A finite selection of eigenfunctions gives a compression, not an exact replacement of the full Hilbert space; a continuous spectrum needs its spectral integrals. This equivalence concerns representations of specified operators, and does not remove the ordering question when quantizing an arbitrary classical expression, as Weyl ordering illustrates.

Exciton

Words: 2k Articles: 27
Quasiparticle OurBigBook.com
An exciton is a bound state of an electron and an electron hole. Their opposite electric charges attract through the Coulomb potential, producing a neutral quasiparticle with internal relative motion and motion of its center of mass. In a semiconductor, promoting an electron from the valence band into the conduction band leaves an electron hole; the pair can occupy either an exciton bound state or an unbound scattering state. Merely creating the two charge carriers does not establish binding. A neutral exciton can transport excitation energy without transporting net electric charge. Coupling this material excitation strongly to a photon can form a polariton.
The striking optical consequence is that an exciton optical transition can absorb a photon with less energy than the threshold for creating unbound electrons and electron holes. The difference is the exciton binding energy, not an extra one-electron energy band inside the band gap. The Wannier-Mott exciton supplies a useful large-radius model; the Frenkel exciton describes the opposite, tightly localized limit.[ref]

A Wannier-Mott exciton has an internal wave function extending over many unit cells. Replace microscopic crystal forces by those effective masses and dielectric screening, and neglect exchange corrections and coupling to phonons. These assumptions must hold on the spatial and energy scales of the particular exciton.

The Bohr radius aB∗​ is a wave function scale, not the radius of a classical orbit; for this model's lowest internal bound state, the mean separation is 3aB∗​/2.
For the diagrams' hypothetical inputs me∗​=0.10m0​, mh∗​=0.40m0​, ϵr​=10 and Eg​=1.500eV, where m0​ is the free electron mass, independent substitution gives μ=0.080m0​, aB∗​≃6.615nm and R∗≃10.885meV. If the relevant energy band edges have different values of crystal momentum, a phonon can also be needed to conserve crystal momentum; subtracting a binding scale from a band gap alone does not specify the optical threshold.

Controls mattered: restricting broadband illumination improved resolution of high-n excitons; lowering laser power or expanding its spot reduced interaction-induced suppression. Electric-dipole selection rules favor P-envelope states in this material, unlike the hypothetical permitted lowest-state transition above. Finite resolution and crystal inhomogeneity affect spectral lines; the inferred binding series requires a continuum threshold and a model.[ref]

Electron hole

Words: 961 Articles: 12
Quasiparticle OurBigBook.com
An electron hole is an unoccupied electron quantum state in an otherwise nearly full energy band, often the valence band. “Filled” refers to occupation of the allowed quantum states, not to filling all space with a continuous fluid of electrons. Each state, including its spin label, can hold at most one electron by the Pauli exclusion principle. The almost full energy band and its few missing occupants are therefore simpler to describe as a background plus a few electron holes. The electron hole is a quasiparticle, not a Positron inserted into the crystal.
Removing an electron of electric charge −e changes the background's electric charge by +e. Thus an electron hole carries positive electric charge relative to that background. Promoting an electron into the conduction band creates an electron hole without changing the whole crystal's electric charge: (−e)+(+e)=0. An unbound pair still consists of two separate charge carriers; only a bound state of their relative motion is an exciton.
The local cartoon explains why a vacancy can move: when a neighboring electron fills it, another vacancy appears where that electron was. The vacancy has moved opposite to that particular transfer of an electron. In an extended Bloch state, use crystal momentum instead of imagining a permanently empty atomic site. For a completely filled energy band the summed electric current vanishes. Omitting one electron with group velocity vv​ removes its contribution −evv​, leaving a contribution +evv​. This fixes both the positive electric charge and the velocity convention of the electron hole.
More precisely, near a parabolic valence band maximum, set its energy Ev​(0) as reference and define the electron hole wave vector by kh​=−kv​. Then
Eh​(kh​)=Ev​(0)−Ev​(−kh​),vh​=ℏ1​∇kh​​Eh​=vv​(−kh​),Eh​(kh​)≃2mh∗​ℏ2kh2​​.
(23)
The occupied electron branch has negative curvature there, while the electron hole branch has positive effective mass mh∗​. The velocity equality compares the electron hole with the missing Bloch state's group velocity; it does not contradict the opposite vacancy motion in a local transfer cartoon. The sign conventions are listed in Phys 460 Lecture 17.

An electron-hole pair consists of an excited electron and the unoccupied valence state described as an electron hole. Electron-hole recombination

Words: 276 Articles: 3
Electron hole OurBigBook.com
An electron filling an electron hole removes both excitations relative to the filled-band background. Their electric charges cancel, consistent with charge conservation; the remaining electrons are still present. The released energy can leave through photon emission or other channels, including phonons. Formation of an exciton instead retains the excited electron and electron hole as a bound pair; recombination removes the pair. A valence band electron filling a nearby vacancy merely moves the electron hole and does not remove the total vacancy count.

Traps and spatial transport can make a single exponential inadequate.

Near the zone centre of many cubic semiconductors, the upper valence bands have different curvatures and hence different band effective masses. Sudden approximation

Words: 2k Articles: 12
Quantum mechanics OurBigBook.com
The sudden approximation treats a rapid, finite change of a Hamiltonian operator as leaving the quantum state approximately unchanged during the switch. The energy measurement can nevertheless change immediately: the same quantum state has different probability amplitudes in the new eigenbasis. Compute their inner products with the new energy eigenstates, then apply the Born rule. The two-level sudden quench below makes this distinction quantitative without assuming the change is small.
An ideal finite step has exact quantum state continuity at a finite Hamiltonian step; a finite-duration implementation has a small evolution error under the bounded-model conditions below. An impulsive quantum kick is different: its Hamiltonian operator grows as its duration shrinks, retaining a finite integrated action and a finite change of quantum state. A sudden approximation therefore concerns short evolution during switching, not conservation of energy during externally driven change. The subsequent unitary time evolution can be substantial.[ref]

Sudden approximation OurBigBook.com
For a fixed Hilbert space, a bounded self-adjoint Hamiltonian operator with a finite step Hi​→Hf​ at t=0 does not deliver an instantaneous rotation of the quantum state. Integrating the Schrödinger equation across a short interval gives
∣ψ(ϵ)⟩−∣ψ(−ϵ)⟩=−ℏi​∫−ϵϵ​H(t)∣ψ(t)⟩dt.
(25)
For a normalized quantum state and ∥H(t)∥≤M in operator norm, the difference has norm at most 2ϵM/ℏ, which tends to zero. The time derivative can jump even though the quantum state is continuous. Here ℏ is the reduced Planck constant. An instantaneous replacement of the eigenbasis changes coordinates, not the vector being represented.
For a real switch occupying 0≤t≤τ, remove any real scalar contribution a(t)I that produces only a global phase, and write ∣ψ​(t)⟩=ei∫0t​a(s)ds/ℏ∣ψ(t)⟩. The same integral argument gives the sufficient bounded-model estimate
​ψ​(τ)−ψ(0)​≤ε,ε=ℏ1​∫0τ​∥H(t)−a(t)I∥dt.
(26)
Thus ε≪1 controls the sudden approximation up to a global phase. For any normalized final energy eigenstate, its probability amplitude differs from the instantaneous-switch value by at most ε, and its Born rule probability differs by at most 2ε. These are sufficient error bounds, not necessary criteria. For the fixed-gap two-level sudden quench, any switching path H(t)=−Δn(t)⋅σ/2 with a unit vector n(t) has operator norm Δ/2, giving ε≤Δτ/(2ℏ).
This estimate is deliberately for bounded Hamiltonian operators. An unbounded energy spectrum does not supply a finite global M; relevant quantum states, operator domains and excited energy eigenvalues require separate control. The adiabatic theorem also requires hypotheses about the path and its spectral gaps; there is no universal switch-duration criterion covering all spectra. The cold-atom collapse and revival after a lattice quench illustrates how a single switch can be sudden for one degree of freedom and slow for another.

Quantum quench OurBigBook.com
A concrete quantum quench experiment loaded a Bose-Einstein condensate of 87Rb chemical atoms from a magnetic field trap into an optical lattice: three orthogonal 838nm laser standing waves, with approximately 125μm beam waists. The switch preserved atom-number populations rather than freezing every motional degree of freedom.[ref]
After variable hold times, releasing the traps and taking photon absorption images after 16ms of flight revealed disappearance and return of interference peaks. Background-subtracted peak counts supplied a coherent fraction. Varying final depth tested the predicted revival period h/U; varying initial depth tested the collapse's sensitivity to atom-number statistics. Peak broadening outside counting windows and spatial variation of U limited later signals.[ref]
Here U is the on-site interaction energy. The approximate isolated-well Hamiltonian operator H=Un^(n^−1)/2, with number operator n^, gives different quantum phases to its number states, which later rephase. This is a many-level realization of the distinction between fixed populations and changing quantum phases.[ref]

Berry phase (γ)

Words: 830 Articles: 5
Quantum mechanics OurBigBook.com
A Berry phase is the geometric phase acquired when a nondegenerate energy eigenstate follows a closed cycle of parameters of a Hamiltonian operator in the ideal limit of the adiabatic theorem. The energy eigenstate must stay separated from other energy eigenstates by a nonzero spectral gap, and the parameters must change sufficiently slowly. Returning the Hamiltonian operator to its starting value returns the state to the same ray, but its quantum phase can remember the journey. The total quantum phase contains both the dynamical phase and the Berry phase.
The beauty of the Berry phase is that, within the adiabatic theorem's limit, it depends on the oriented path of the parameters rather than how long the journey takes. For a spin one-half qubit, the Berry phase of a Bloch-sphere latitude turns that memory into half a solid angle. Berry-phase interference with a reference path converts this geometry into a detection probability.
Michael Berry's 1984 paper formulated the geometric phase for cycles governed by the adiabatic theorem and derived the solid angle result for spin. Its bibliographic details are Proceedings of the Royal Society of London A, volume 392, pages 45–57, DOI 10.1098/rspa.1984.0023. [ref]; [ref]. The wider concept of geometric phase does not require every cycle to obey the adiabatic theorem: Aharonov and Anandan formulated a geometric phase for general cyclic quantum evolution in 1987. [ref].

This is the +1 eigenstate of n⋅σ, where σ are the Pauli matrices. To make it an instantaneous ground state, take the model Hamiltonian operator H=−Δn⋅σ/2 with constant Δ>0. Its energy eigenvalues are −Δ/2 and +Δ/2, so its spectral gap is Δ everywhere. The spin points along n; this explicit convention fixes the sign of the Berry phase.
Keep the polar angle θ fixed and increase the azimuth ϕ from 0 to 2π, slowly enough for the adiabatic theorem. The state vector written above is periodic in ϕ. Directly differentiating gives
∂ϕ​∣ψ⟩=ieiϕsin2θ​∣1⟩,⟨ψ∣∂ϕ​ψ⟩=isin22θ​.

At θ=60∘, the solid angle is π and the Berry phase is −π/2. At θ=90∘, the solid angle is 2π and the Berry phase is −π. At θ=0, the loop collapses and γ=0. At θ=π, the same expression gives −2π≡0: the Bloch vector stays at the south pole, while this representative is eiϕ∣1⟩. Its winding is only a choice of global phase, so the physically relevant phase factor is again one. The displayed formula is a continuous, unwrapped representative, not a unique real-valued observable.

In one arm the internal spin one-half qubit follows the loop; in the reference arm it stays in its starting energy eigenstate. Assume equal arm amplitudes, identical final internal states, cancelled relative dynamical phases, and calibrated fixed apparatus phases. In the model above, hold the reference Hamiltonian operator at its initial value for the same duration. Both arms then have energy eigenvalue −Δ/2 and acquire the same dynamical phase ΔT/(2ℏ), so their relative dynamical phase vanishes in the ideal limit of the adiabatic theorem.
The joint quantum state before recombination then factors as

Photoelectric effect

Words: 2k Articles: 10
Photon absorption OurBigBook.com
The photoelectric effect is the release of electrons from matter following photon absorption. Here the focus is emission from a metal surface into vacuum: a photon supplies energy, the work function pays the escape cost, and the remainder can become the emitted electron's kinetic energy. A photocurrent counts collected electric charge; a stopping potential probes the upper kinetic energy limit. These are different measurements.
In 1905, Albert Einstein proposed that an individual light quantum could transfer its whole energy to one electron. His §8 allowed losses before escape, distinguished the fastest emitted electrons from the rest, and predicted a straight stopping potential versus frequency relation with a material-independent slope. He separately predicted that changing light intensity changes the number emitted without changing their velocity distribution under otherwise identical conditions. He also discussed incomplete transfer and limits to the account.[ref]
The useful modern starting model is a clean, homogeneous metal with independent single-photon events, negligible initial thermal broadening, negligible lowering of the surface barrier by an applied electric field, and negligible electric fields from the emitted electrons themselves. Specify the surface and its work function; it is not enough to name the bulk material. The Einstein photoelectric equation describes the upper edge of the emission energy distribution. It neither predicts that every absorbed photon liberates an electron nor supplies the whole photocurrent curve. Its appeal is that a complicated surface process still exposes the universal Planck constant through a simple slope.

An electron at the highest occupied energy can reach this edge if it escapes without an additional loss. An electron starting lower or losing energy within the metal emerges below it. The material takes recoil momentum; its recoil energy is neglected in this model.
For an original chosen example, take Φ=2.30eV and ν=8.00×1014Hz. Using h=6.62607015×10−34Js and the elementary charge e=1.602176634×10−19C gives hν=3.308534eV and Kmax​=1.008534eV. The ideal stopping potential is therefore 1.008534V. At 4.00×1014Hz the same model supplies only 1.654267eV per photon, so this single-photon channel is closed. A negative result from hν−Φ means no emission through that channel, not an emitted electron with negative kinetic energy.

Photoelectric saturation current (Isat​=eηP/(hν))
Words: 197
Photoelectric effect OurBigBook.com
The photoelectric saturation current is the photocurrent reached when increasing the collecting electric potential difference no longer increases the fraction of available emitted electrons collected. It is saturation with collecting voltage at fixed illumination. It does not mean that increasing incident light intensity cannot increase emission.
If P is incident radiant flux on the emitting area and η is the external quantum efficiency for producing escaping electrons, then the incident photon arrival rate is P/(hν) and complete collection gives Isat​=eηP/(hν). For the example's ν=8.00×1014Hz, choose η=0.10 and P=1.00μW. The calculated photon arrival rate is 1.886488×1012s−1 and Isat​=30.224866nA. Doubling P doubles this current to 60.449731nA while leaving Vs​ fixed. At fixed illuminated area this doubles the irradiance. Changing frequency at fixed P changes the arrival rate as well as the photon energy; η can also change, so there is no general rule that a higher frequency gives a larger photocurrent.
A missing plateau can indicate incomplete collection or an electric field altered by the emitted electric charge. Heating, surface changes and additional emission channels can invalidate a constant η. Even a small amount of unwanted higher-frequency radiation can move an apparent endpoint. A stopping potential inferred from zero net current additionally needs background subtraction and a check for emission from the collector itself.
Millikan photoelectric experiment
Words: 489 Articles: 2
Photoelectric effect OurBigBook.com
Robert Andrews Millikan's 1916 experiment used a magnetically turned wheel and rotary knife to expose sodium or lithium in vacuum. A surrounding copper-gauze/solid-copper collector caught electrons; an electrometer recorded accumulated electric charge over thirty seconds at each applied voltage. He located endpoints graphically from photocurrent curves. Mercury spectral lines, selected by a monochromator and filters, controlled frequency; rejecting shorter-wavelength contamination protected the endpoint. An oxidized collector suppressed reverse emission for selected lines. A copper test plate measured the contact potential difference by a displacement-null method; a certified voltmeter set the electrical scale. He compared stable-surface sweeps with rapid alternating-frequency measurements to control drift. The slope tested h/e; the threshold required the contact correction. His gauge did not measure mercury vapor. Confirmation of the equation coexisted with his continued skepticism about localized light quanta.[ref]
For a modern repetition of the logic, first establish electrical zero with the illumination blocked, characterize leakage, and verify the voltmeter scale independently of the presumed Planck constant. Scan several voltages near each endpoint rather than calling one noisy zero a cutoff. Hold the illuminated area and surface state fixed when varying light intensity; vary frequency independently when testing the slope. Repeating a reference frequency between other readings reveals time-dependent offsets. Agreement of a slope with h/e tests an energy relation; it does not alone identify every microscopic step of photon absorption and escape.

Surface condition and different work functions can create a vacuum gap field even when an external voltmeter reads zero. Connecting the metals establishes equilibrium of their electronic chemical potentials including electrostatic energy; it need not equalize the electrostatic electric potential in the gap.

Their difference is 1.654267V, giving h/e≃4.135668×10−15Vs. Ignoring Vc​ in the intercept would falsely infer 2.50eV for the work function. Thus increasing light intensity below the single-photon threshold cannot open that single-photon channel, but can make other channels relevant. Quantum mechanics OurBigBook.com
A free particle has no potential energy, so its Hamiltonian is H=p2/(2m). On unbounded Euclidean space its energy spectrum has no normalizable lowest-energy eigenstate.

Ground state

Words: 2k Articles: 10
Quantum mechanics OurBigBook.com
A ground state is a normalized energy eigenstate that attains the lowest possible energy of a quantum system. Precisely, let the Hamiltonian operator H be a self-adjoint operator bounded below on a Hilbert space, and write E∗​=infσ(H) for the infimum of its spectrum. A ground state is a unit vector ψ0​ in the operator domain D(H) satisfying
Hψ0​=E∗​ψ0​,∥ψ0​∥=1.
(52)
Thus a ground state exists exactly when the spectral bottom E∗​ is an energy eigenvalue. The lowest energy eigenvalue among some listed bound states is insufficient if other parts of the spectrum lie below it. The ground-state subspace collects all minimizing energy eigenstates; it can have ground-state degeneracy. The quantum variational principle characterizes E∗​ as the infimum of normalized energy expectation values. [ref].
For the one-dimensional quantum harmonic oscillator, the ground state has energy ℏω/2 above the minimum of the potential energy. This zero-point energy is compatible with being the lowest allowed energy: a localized wavefunction cannot simultaneously have zero kinetic energy. For a free particle on the whole line, the spectral bottom is zero but is unattained by any normalizable wavefunction; see ground-state energy. A lower bound therefore need not describe a physically preparable energy eigenstate.
The ground state supplies a reference for excitation costs and for the quantum variational principle. A ground state is also a stationary state under a time-independent Hamiltonian operator: its quantum phase changes, while its position probability density stays fixed. A nonzero ground-state energy does not imply motion along a classical trajectory, and ground-state degeneracy means there need not be a unique lowest quantum state.

Ground state OurBigBook.com
The probability that an energy measurement selects a ground state. For a nondegenerate normalized mode ϕ1​, it is ∣⟨ϕ1​,ψ⟩∣2; for a degenerate ground eigenspace, use its full orthogonal projection.

Ground-state subspace (ker(H−E0​I))

Words: 39
Ground state OurBigBook.com
The ground-state subspace is the eigenspace of a Hamiltonian operator at its lowest eigenvalue E0​. A computational history state construction can have many valid quantum witnesses, hence a degenerate ground space. Perturbation bounds must optimize on this entire subspace, rather than on a chosen basis of ground states.

Ground-state degeneracy

Words: 277
Ground state OurBigBook.com
When a ground state exists, its ground-state degeneracy is the dimension of the ground-state subspace:
g0​=dimker(H−E0​I),E0​=infσ(H).
(53)
Here I is the identity operator, and the kernel of a linear map is taken within the operator domain of the Hamiltonian operator H. The count concerns linearly independent energy eigenstates, rather than every normalized quantum superposition or every choice of global phase. Even a single energy eigenspace contains infinitely many representing vectors; its dimension measures independent freedom. Ground-state degeneracy is the lowest-energy instance of degenerate energy levels.
For an exact finite model with energy unit ε>0, let the Hamiltonian operator be the diagonal matrix
Htoy​=εdiag(0,0,2,5).
(54)
Its ground-state energy is zero and g0​=2: the first two coordinate unit vectors e1​,e2​ span the ground-state subspace. Every normalized ae1​+be2​, with ∣a∣2+∣b∣2=1, is a ground state, including (e1​+e2​)/2​. Its energy measurement is certain to return zero, even though a measurement distinguishing e1​ from e2​ need not have a definite outcome. Under the unchanged Hamiltonian operator, this quantum superposition is a stationary state because both components acquire the same global phase.
Ground-state degeneracy matters when an interaction selects or splits previously equal energy eigenvalues. In the finite model, adding εdiag(δ,−δ,0,0) with 0<δ<2 gives the formerly lowest pair the distinct energies ±εδ, leaving a unique ground state. This direct calculation illustrates why degenerate perturbation theory first examines the perturbation inside the whole ground-state subspace.
A classical continuous-symmetry model can instead have a manifold of minimizing configurations, such as the sphere of orientations of a Néel state in an isotropic Heisenberg antiferromagnet. That geometric description does not by itself count the dimension of a finite quantum ground-state subspace.

Ground state OurBigBook.com
The ground-state energy E0​ is the energy eigenvalue attained by a ground state. For a self-adjoint operator H bounded below, distinguish this attained value from the always-defined spectral bottom E∗​=infσ(H). When a ground state exists, E0​=E∗​. Some usage calls E∗​ the ground-state energy even when it is unattained; here an unattained bottom is explicitly identified as an infimum. The quantum variational principle states
E∗​=infψ∈D(H)∥ψ∥=1​​⟨ψ,Hψ⟩.
(55)
Approaching this infimum with trial wavefunctions does not ensure that a minimizing wavefunction exists. [ref].
For the whole-line free particle with mass m>0,
H=−2mℏ2​dx2d2​,σ(H)=[0,∞).
(56)
Its spectrum is continuous and contains no energy eigenvalues represented by normalizable wavefunctions. The Fourier transform makes H multiplication by ℏ2k2/(2m); a fixed energy restricts k to a set of zero length, on which a nonzero square-integrable function cannot be supported. [ref]. An explicit family of normalized Gaussian wave packets demonstrates how the bottom is approached:

The formula follows from ψs′​=−xψs​/(2s2), integration by parts, and ⟨x2⟩s​=s2. Every finite width gives positive kinetic energy. At zero energy, Hψ=0 would require an affine function on the whole line, which is never a nonzero normalizable wavefunction. Spreading a Gaussian wave packet indefinitely produces an unattained infimum, rather than a zero-energy ground state.
An additive choice of energy origin changes the numerical ground-state energy without changing the ground-state subspace. For H′=H+CI, every energy eigenvalue becomes E′=E+C, while all differences Ej​−Ei​ stay fixed. Time evolution gains only the global phase e−iCt/ℏ. This makes excitation costs and spectroscopic differences more intrinsic than the isolated number E0​.

The quantum variational principle estimates the lowest energy by choosing a trial wavefunction and computing its expectation value, without solving the Schrödinger equation exactly. Minimizing over a manageable family of trial wavefunctions gives an upper bound; enlarging that family can improve the estimate.
Let H be a self-adjoint operator bounded below, and put E∗​=infσ(H). For ∥ψ∥=1 in its operator domain D(H),

(58)
Trial states may also lie in the form domain Q(H)=D((H−bI)1/2), where b≤E∗​. Then use the quadratic form of a positive quantum Hamiltonian shifted by b:

(59)
This extends the expectation value beyond D(H) without requiring Hψ to exist. Equality for a normalized state holds exactly in the energy eigenspace at E∗​, if that eigenvalue exists. [ref].
A short proof makes the direction of the bound memorable. If H has a complete orthonormal basis of energy eigenstates ϕn​, write
ψ=∑n​cn​ϕn​,Hϕn​=En​ϕn​,∑n​∣cn​∣2=1.
(60)
The expectation value is a weighted average of allowed energies:
qH​[ψ]−E∗​=∑n​∣cn​∣2(En​−E∗​)≥0.
(61)
Equality requires every occupied energy eigenstate to have energy E∗​. [ref]. With continuous spectrum, the spectral theorem replaces the sum by an integral against the scalar spectral measure; the same nonnegative-difference argument works.
For an unnormalized trial wavefunction, divide by its squared norm: RH​[ψ]=qH​[ψ]/∥ψ∥2 is the form version of the Rayleigh quotient. The quantum variational principle supplies an upper bound on E∗​; it supplies neither a lower bound on E∗​ nor, by itself, a guarantee that a bound state exists.

Quantum tunnelling

Quantum tunnelling is transmission through a potential barrier even when the particle energy is below the barrier height.
The wavefunction penetrates the classically inaccessible region; matching it to an outgoing scattering state on the far side gives a nonzero transmission probability. For a real, time-independent potential barrier, the transmitted energy equals the incident energy: quantum tunnelling does not require a temporary violation of conservation of energy. A tunnel junction turns this small transmission probability into a measurable electric current, whose sensitivity to separation makes the scanning tunnelling microscope possible.

Here R=∣r∣2 is the quantum reflection probability, and T=Jtr​/Jinc​ is the transmission probability. Current-distance test of vacuum tunnelling

Words: 717 Articles: 10
Quantum tunnelling OurBigBook.com
Tunneling through a controllable vacuum gap by Gerd Binnig and others made barrier width experimentally adjustable. Their apparatus used a pointed electrical conductor opposite a conducting plate, with fine positioning by piezoelectricity. Rubber-tube support and magnetic levitation above a cooled bowl exhibiting superconductivity suppressed vibrations; the junction itself remained near room temperature.[ref]
The readout was electrical resistance versus displacement at a fixed electric potential difference of 60 mV of either polarity. They observed an exponential function dependence spanning four orders of magnitude. Cleaning and better vacuum increased the inferred barrier from approximately 0.6-0.7 eV to 3.2 eV. Reproducible curves and the cleaning response argued against deforming contamination layers; an appropriate slope also helped exclude an ordinary conducting contact. The paper reports residual contamination, electronics-limited range and a jump attributed to release of thermal stress; its curve origins generally do not determine absolute gap widths.[ref]
The ideal tunnel junction model explains the slope. At fixed small electric potential difference, fixed tip geometry and approximately unchanged density of states, take an effective barrier energy Φ above the relevant electron states and approximate the current magnitude by
I(s)≃Cexp(−2κs),κ=ℏ2me​Φ​​,−dsdlnI​≃2κ.
(81)
The coefficient C includes the applied electric potential difference, available occupied and empty quantum states, and tip geometry. A single transmission probability is not an electric current: a junction combines contributions from many electron states in both directions, with the electric potential difference producing a net imbalance. Its tilted, material-dependent barrier is only approximated by the equal-exterior rectangular potential barrier; the exact single-particle formula above is not a complete junction model.
For the chosen model value Φ=4 electronvolts, κ≃10.25nm−1. Increasing separation by 0.1nm multiplies I by about 0.129, a reduction by about 7.8. The following diagram chooses I(0.4nm)=1nA solely for illustration; it contains no measured data and is not a fit to the 1982 curves.
Distance calibration is essential. In Scanning Tunneling Microscopy: From Birth to Adolescence by Gerd Binnig and others, the authors describe an initial inferred barrier near 1 eV. Recalibration found only half the quoted piezo displacement sensitivity and raised the inferred barrier above 4 eV. Thus an exponential trace alone was insufficient evidence for tunnelling through vacuum. The model makes the sensitivity explicit: the inferred Φ=ℏ2(dlnI/ds)2/(8me​) depends quadratically on the distance scale.[ref]
For scanning tunnelling microscopy, feedback control adjusts the vertical position to hold electric current fixed during a lateral scan; the recorded height follows separation only when the surface is electronically homogeneous. Changes in the local density of states can also change apparent height. This limitation is already explicit in the authors' account of constant-current imaging.[ref]

On 0<β<π/2, these equations reduce to β/cosβ=ρ. The left side is continuous, strictly increasing from zero to infinity, with derivative secβ(1+βtanβ)>0. The intermediate value theorem gives exactly one root on this first branch for every ρ>0. It has 0<β<ρ, hence α>0 and −V0​<E<0. The matched cosine interior and exponential tails therefore give a nonzero even square-integrable function with continuous first derivative, which can be normalized. As the well becomes shallow the binding energy approaches zero but remains negative; see shallow finite-square-well energy.

Each energy eigenstate has n−1 interior nodes of a standing wave, at x=jL/n for j=1,…,n−1. More curvature costs more kinetic energy, explaining the n2 growth. The positive ground-state energy is a confinement effect: a constant zero-energy wavefunction cannot satisfy both walls and remain normalized.
For an electron with mass me​=9.1093837139×10−31kg in a box of length L=1nm, use h=6.62607015×10−34Js and 1eV=1.602176634×10−19J. These constants are from the 2022 CODATA adjustment. [ref]. Substitution gives

Doubling L quarters every energy eigenvalue; doubling m halves them. This scaling makes the particle in a box useful for estimating confinement energies before attempting a more realistic calculation. A finite square well permits exterior tails for bound states and has only finitely many bound energy eigenstates. For an electron, the scalar box calculation assumes fixed spin and no spin-dependent interactions.
For the ground state, the probability of finding the particle in the middle half of the box is fully computable:
Pr(4L​<x<43L​)=∫L/43L/4​L2​sin2Lπx​dx=[Lx​−2πsin(2πx/L)​]L/43L/4​=21​+π1​≈0.818310.

An equal quantum superposition of the first two energy eigenstates gives a simple example of moving density:

A mixed state describing a statistical mixture with those populations has the constant probability density (ϕ12​+ϕ22​)/2; it lacks this matter-wave interference term.

Expanding a state in unperturbed energy eigenstates with their free phases converts the time-dependent Schrodinger equation into coupled equations for slowly varying amplitudes. To first order, the perturbation on the right-hand side acts on the initial unperturbed state.

Electric-dipole approximation (Hint​≃−d⋅E(R,t))

Words: 110
Electric-dipole interaction OurBigBook.com
For a localized charge distribution in an external field varying little across its extent, expand the external scalar potential about a reference point R. The constant term couples to total charge; the first spatially varying term gives the electric-dipole interaction −d⋅E(R,t), where d is the electric dipole moment. Higher spatial multipoles are neglected.
For a passing charge at minimum distance b, the atomic extent must be small compared with b. For a plane electromagnetic wave, the analogous long-wavelength condition is ka≪1, as in the electric-dipole approximation for radiation. A short interaction time and a spatially uniform field across the atom are different assumptions; neither implies the other.

Electric-dipole selection rule

Words: 133 Articles: 3
Electric-dipole interaction OurBigBook.com
Because the position operator has odd parity, an electric-dipole matrix element vanishes between states of the same parity. For orbital-angular-momentum eigenstates, the full rule is Δℓ=±1 and Δm=0,±1, with the field polarization selecting the allowed change in m.
First-order parity selection in an infinite well
Words: 67 Articles: 1
Electric-dipole selection rule OurBigBook.com
For 0<x<w, normalized states ψn​=2/w​sin[(n+1)πx/w] have centre-reflection eigenvalue (−1)n. Since x−w/2 is odd, off-diagonal electric-dipole matrix elements vanish between equal-parity states. Ground state n=0 cannot reach n=2 at first order; an initial n=1 can reach even labels including n=0. This does not impose an all-orders prohibition: two dipole interactions can restore the original parity. The general nonzero elements follow from position matrix elements in a symmetric infinite square well after shifting the origin.

Laporte rule
Words: 25
Electric-dipole selection rule OurBigBook.com
For an inversion-symmetric system, electric-dipole transitions require opposite parities. Transitions between d-shell terms of the same gerade parity can acquire weak vibronic or symmetry-breaking intensity.

For a harmonic perturbation and continuum detuning Ω(k), first-order amplitudes contain
Ω(k)/2sin(Ω(k)t/2)​.
(133)
The distributional limit
(Ω/2)2sin2(Ωt/2)​⟶2πtδ(Ω)

selects energy-conserving continuum states and produces a transition probability linear in time.

Time-independent perturbation theory

Words: 693 Articles: 15
Quantum mechanics OurBigBook.com
Time-independent perturbation theory expands the eigenvalues and eigenstates of H0​+V in powers of a small perturbation V.
This is the stationary branch of perturbation theory.

Linear confinement correction to Coulomb bound states (ΔEnl​=b⟨r⟩nl​)

Words: 56
Time-independent perturbation theory OurBigBook.com
For reduced mass μ and Coulomb strength a, put aq​=ℏ2/(μa). The perturbation br shifts the 1s,2s,2p energies by 3baq​/2,6baq​,5baq​, respectively. These values follow by integrating r3∣Rnl​∣2. Because the perturbation is central, angular orthogonality makes its matrix diagonal inside each Coulomb energy eigenspace. It splits the accidental degeneracy between different orbital angular momenta while preserving magnetic degeneracy.

Gaussian perturbation of a quantum harmonic oscillator (ΔE1​/ΔE0​=α2/(α2+β2))

Words: 47
Time-independent perturbation theory OurBigBook.com
For perturbation V0​e−β2x2 and oscillator inverse length α=mω/ℏ​, direct Gaussian expectation values give ΔE0​=V0​α/(α2+β2)1/2 and ΔE1​=V0​α3/(α2+β2)3/2. A narrow perturbation samples the odd state's node and suppresses its shift by two extra powers of α/β. A broad perturbation approaches a constant energy offset for both states.

Nondegenerate perturbation theory

Words: 142 Articles: 2
Time-independent perturbation theory OurBigBook.com
Perturbation theory for an isolated eigenvalue with a one-dimensional eigenspace. First-order nondegenerate perturbation theory gives the diagonal perturbation expectation, while second-order nondegenerate perturbation theory accounts for coupling to other unperturbed eigenstates through energy denominators. Symmetry can permit its use within one block even if another, uncoupled symmetry block has the same unperturbed eigenvalue.

Cosine perturbation of the ground level in a one-dimensional box (E=2ma2π2ℏ2​−2ϵ​−16π2ℏ2ma2ϵ2​+O(ϵ3))

Words: 61
Nondegenerate perturbation theory OurBigBook.com
For the normalized sine eigenfunctions of a particle in a box on (0,a), multiplying the lowest one by ϵcos(2πx/a) gives ϵ(ϕ3​−ϕ1​)/2. Thus the first-order diagonal shift is −ϵ/2, and the only second-order coupling is to level three. With E3​=9E1​, its contribution is (ϵ2/4)/(E1​−E3​)=−ϵ2/(32E1​), giving the displayed expansion. This simple selection rule makes the full second-order perturbation theory sum a single term.

Perturbative mixing parameter

Words: 39
Nondegenerate perturbation theory OurBigBook.com
The ratio ∣⟨k∣V∣i⟩/(Ei​−Ek​)∣ measures a leading admixture between unperturbed eigenstates. Small matrix elements compared with relevant gaps justify a nondegenerate expansion locally. A small overall perturbation does not suffice near a coupled degeneracy, where the nearly degenerate block needs diagonalization.

Hellmann–Feynman theorem (E′(λ)=⟨ψ,H′(λ)ψ⟩)

Words: 49
Time-independent perturbation theory OurBigBook.com
For a differentiable normalized eigenstate of a differentiable self-adjoint Hamiltonian, differentiate Hψ=Eψ and pair with ψ. The terms involving ψ′ cancel because H is self-adjoint, leaving the stated formula. It turns energy derivatives into observable expectations. A smoothly chosen eigenbranch and suitable operator-domain regularity are required, particularly at degeneracies or crossings.

First-order energy correction (En(1)​)

Words: 157 Articles: 1
Time-independent perturbation theory OurBigBook.com
The first-order energy correction is the coefficient of the perturbation parameter in the expansion of an energy eigenvalue.

Apparent level crossing from a finite-interval oscillator perturbation (H′=21​mω2(a2−x2)1[−a,a]​)

Words: 139
First-order energy correction OurBigBook.com
Let σ2=ℏ/(2mω) and g(x)=(2πσ2)−1/2e−x2/(2σ2) be the quantum harmonic oscillator ground-state probability density. Put p(a)=∫−aa​g(x)dx. The first excited-state density is x2g(x)/σ2. Integration by parts, using g′=−xg/σ2, gives the first-order difference
E1′​−E0′​=−2ℏω​[p(a)−2ag(a)].
(135)
The bracket grows from zero to one, since its derivative is 2a2g(a)/σ2. Thus the first-order predicted level gap for H0​+λH′ is ℏω[1−λ{p(a)−2ag(a)}/2]. For every λ>2 it becomes negative at sufficiently large a.
For λ>1 the full potential has a central barrier and symmetric minima at ±a. The unperturbed even ground state samples the central barrier more strongly than the odd excited state, whose node reduces its shift. This explains the perturbative tendency, but the negative predicted gap is a failure diagnostic of the first-order truncation. The exact one-dimensional ground state remains nodeless and below the first excited state; in a high symmetric barrier the actual pair has a small positive double-well tunneling splitting.

An energy eigenvalue is nondegenerate when its eigenspace is one-dimensional. Its normalized eigenstate is then unique up to a complex phase.

(A+A†)4∣0⟩=3∣0⟩+62​∣2⟩+26​∣4⟩,

For a normalized nondegenerate eigenstate ∣n⟩,
En(2)​=∑m=n​En(0)​−Em(0)​∣⟨m∣V∣n⟩∣2​.

Words: 44
Second-order nondegenerate perturbation theory OurBigBook.com
For a nondegenerate lowest state, every excited-state denominator E0​−Ek​ is negative. Since each numerator ∣Vk0​∣2 is nonnegative, their sum is nonpositive, and strictly negative if a coupled higher state exists. The statement assumes the perturbative expansion and appropriate sum or spectral integral are defined.

For
H=(E−​iλ​−iλE+​​),Δ=E+​−E−​>0,

Bright and dark state reduction of a star-coupled Hamiltonian

Words: 68
Time-independent perturbation theory OurBigBook.com
Suppose one state ∣0⟩ couples to degenerate states ∣1⟩,…,∣m⟩ with amplitudes v1​,…,vm​, while the degenerate states do not couple to each other. The normalized bright state proportional to ∑j​vj​∣j⟩ is the only combination coupled to ∣0⟩. Every orthogonal combination is a dark state and remains an exact eigenstate at the degenerate energy. The remaining spectrum comes from a two-dimensional Hamiltonian whose off-diagonal entry is (∑j​∣vj​∣2)1/2.

Degenerate perturbation theory

Words: 524 Articles: 10
Quantum mechanics OurBigBook.com
First-order degenerate perturbation theory diagonalizes the perturbing operator within each degenerate eigenspace of the unperturbed Hamiltonian.

First-order cancellation for an exchange-odd perturbation (PVP=0)

Words: 83
Degenerate perturbation theory OurBigBook.com
Let X be a unitary operator with X2=I, and let P be the orthogonal projection operator onto an unperturbed energy eigenspace. Suppose X acts as the same sign ε=±1 throughout that eigenspace and XVX=−V. For any u,v in the eigenspace, preservation of the inner product gives ⟨u,Vv⟩=⟨Xu,XVv⟩=−⟨εu,Vεv⟩=−⟨u,Vv⟩. Hence every projected matrix element vanishes, so PVP=0 and degenerate perturbation theory gives zero first-order energy corrections. A zero diagonal alone would be insufficient. For equal spins, the exchange parity of two coupled identical spins is constant on each total-spin sector, while their spin-projection difference changes sign under exchange.

Schrieffer-Wolff transformation

Words: 163 Articles: 3
Degenerate perturbation theory OurBigBook.com
A perturbative unitary conjugation eliminating couplings between chosen separated energy sectors. For H=H0​+V and an anti-Hermitian S satisfying [S,H0​]=−V at leading order, the transformed Hamiltonian contains 21​[S,V] at second order. Exactly resonant coupled states must be retained in a common block. The method was used for the Anderson-to-Kondo relation by John Robert Schrieffer and P. A. Wolff.

Resonance obstruction to perturbative elimination

Words: 46
Schrieffer-Wolff transformation OurBigBook.com
A perturbative generator dividing by an unperturbed energy difference cannot eliminate a nonzero coupling between exactly degenerate states. Those states must remain in the retained degenerate block. Small denominators also invalidate an expansion when the actual hopping matrix element, including occupation enhancement, is not small in comparison.

Schrieffer-Wolff transformation OurBigBook.com
If site-transfer energies are E(Δ), the left-ordered raising-hop generator has coefficient f(Δ)=t/[E(Δ)−E(Δ−2)]. Nonlinear occupation energies generally make the effective second-order shifts and spin-exchange amplitudes depend on the occupation sector.
Occupancy-preserving second-order bosonic hopping (Hocc(2)​=t[f(Δ)XY−f(Δ+2)YX])

Occupation-dependent virtual hopping OurBigBook.com
With X=∑s​as†​bs​, Y=X† and a real coefficient f, the fixed-occupancy second-order operator is t[f(Δ)XY−f(Δ+2)YX]. Normal ordering gives XY=Na​+P and YX=Nb​+P, where P=∑ss′​as†​as′​bs′†​bs​ exchanges internal states without changing site totals.

Equal-coupling three-state perturbation

Words: 45
Degenerate perturbation theory OurBigBook.com
A real perturbation with zero diagonal and every off-diagonal element t has one eigenvalue 2t on the symmetric vector and a twofold eigenvalue −t on its orthogonal complement. It is t(J3​−I), where J3​ is the all-ones matrix. Diagonal entries alone do not give first-order energies in a degenerate subspace.

Degenerate orbital exchange splitting from a product perturbation (δE±​=±α∣⟨r∣x∣s⟩∣2)

Words: 134
Degenerate perturbation theory OurBigBook.com
Two distinguishable particles with equal one-particle spectra have degenerate ordered orbital products ∣r,s⟩ and ∣s,r⟩ for r=s. Suppose both individual position means vanish, as in a centred parity-symmetric well. The perturbation αx1​x2​ then has zero diagonal matrix elements, but its restriction to this two-dimensional subspace is
W=α(0∣xrs​∣2​∣xrs​∣20​),xrs​=⟨r∣x∣s⟩.
(142)
Degenerate perturbation theory gives normalized symmetric and antisymmetric eigenfunctions (∣r,s⟩±∣s,r⟩)/2​ with shifts ±α∣xrs​∣2. Thus vanishing diagonal expectations in a chosen degenerate basis do not imply vanishing first-order energy shifts. Distinguishability permits both exchange symmetries; it does not forbid their energy splitting.
For an infinite square well of width a, the first two orbitals have ∣x12​∣2=256a2/(81π4) by the position matrix elements in a symmetric infinite square well. If the particles are identical spin one-half fermions, the spatially symmetric and antisymmetric combinations must instead be paired with the singlet state and triplet states, respectively. A spin-independent perturbation leaves each allowed spin multiplicity intact.

The Pauli X eigenstates are (∣0⟩±∣1⟩)/2​ with eigenvalues ±1.

Rectangular potential barrier

Words: 136 Articles: 1
Quantum mechanics OurBigBook.com
A rectangular potential barrier has a constant elevated potential over a finite interval and a lower constant potential outside it. Matching wavefunctions and derivatives at the interval endpoints gives its reflection and transmission amplitudes. It is a special potential barrier.

Rectangular-barrier tunnelling probability (T=[1+V02​sinh2(κa)/(4E(V0​−E))]−1)

Words: 100
Rectangular potential barrier OurBigBook.com
For a rectangular potential barrier of height V0​, width a, and equal constant potentials outside, a particle with 0<E<V0​ has exterior wave number k=2mE​/ℏ and interior decay constant κ=2m(V0​−E)​/ℏ. Write the three wavefunctions as eikx+re−ikx, Aeκx+Be−κx, and teikx. Continuity of the wavefunction and its derivative at both interfaces determines the transmission probability T=∣t∣2 in the title. Equal exterior velocities are what permit the last equality.
For κa≫1, sinh2(κa)≃e2κa/4, so
T≃V02​16E(V0​−E)​e−2κa.
(145)
Keeping only e−2κa estimates the exponentially dominant quantum tunnelling suppression; the interface prefactor can still change a numerical answer by a factor of order one.

Perturbation theory (quantum mechanics)

Words: 18
Quantum mechanics OurBigBook.com
Perturbation theory expands a quantum problem around a solvable Hamiltonian. Time-independent perturbation theory expands stationary energies and eigenstates; time-dependent perturbation theory expands dynamical amplitudes and transitions.

Hartree equations

Words: 263 Articles: 5
Quantum mechanics OurBigBook.com
The Hartree equations are self-consistent one-particle equations obtained by approximating a many-body wave function by a tensor product of orbital wave functions. Each orbital sees the potential averaged over the other particles' probability densities; attractive Newtonian mean-field variants include the Gravitational Hartree equation.

Hartree method

Words: 77 Articles: 1
Hartree equations OurBigBook.com
A variational product of one-electron orbitals produces coupled one-electron equations, each containing the electrostatic density of the other occupied orbitals. Iterating orbitals and potentials gives a self-consistent field. The product omits fermionic exchange; an antisymmetric Slater determinant instead leads to Hartree-Fock theory.

Pair-energy double counting in Hartree orbital sums

Words: 38
Hartree method OurBigBook.com
For Hartree direct integrals Jij​ and orbital eigenvalues ϵi​, the product-state energy is E=∑i​ϵi​−∑i<j​Jij​. Each pair enters two orbital mean fields but only once in the total interaction energy. Orbital energies are therefore not independent additive particle energies.

Hartree product state

Words: 63
Hartree equations OurBigBook.com
A many-particle trial state built from one-particle factors, without the additional correlations of a general many-body wavefunction. For identical bosons occupying one normalized orbital φ, the symmetric fixed-number form is (aφ†​)N∣0⟩/N!​. Its field expectation is zero because annihilation changes particle number, while its one-body density matrix has the macroscopic eigenvalue N. An antisymmetrized multi-orbital fermionic trial state instead belongs to the Hartree-Fock construction.

Hartree potential

Words: 90 Articles: 1
Hartree equations OurBigBook.com
The local mean Coulomb potential generated by the occupied electron density. A separate positive background or external charge contribution must be included where appropriate. Hartree-Fock exchange is nonlocal and removes equal-orbital self-interaction from the total direct-plus-exchange result.

Hartree electrostatic energy (EH​=e2/(8πϵ0​)∬n(r)n(r′)/∣r−r′∣d3rd3r′)

Words: 56
Hartree potential OurBigBook.com
The classical electrostatic self-energy functional of an electron number density is the expression in the title. The factor one-half prevents counting each pair twice. Its functional derivative is the Hartree potential; integrating density times that potential gives 2EH​. The functional includes an unphysical one-electron self-interaction unless other terms cancel it. It differs from the Hartree energy atomic unit.
